passages.text: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can scale large language model agents on long-horizon tasks by running them in parallel, yet existing designs waste much of this parallelism in _bubbles_ : agent time spent waiting on others or redoing a peer’s work. These bubbles stem from how agents communicate. Independent agents share nothing and rediscover what their peers have already found; peer-communicating agents wait at synchronous rounds; and under centralized orchestration, the main agent blocks on its sub-agents while progress is relayed. We propose Decentralized Language Models (DELM), a MAS framework on top of existing agent harnesses that squeezes out these bubbles by replacing the main agent with a shared context and a task queue. Agents asynchronously claim tasks, publish findings as soon as they are available, and build on or correct one another’s progress, with every peer’s status visible to all. On long-horizon tasks from Terminal-Bench 4.0 and DeepSWE v1.1, and on SWE-bench Verified, DELM is both more accurate and faster than Codex, Claude Code, their native subagents, and AOrchestra in every setting, improving accuracy by up to 17.5 points over the strongest baseline and running up to 2.49 _×_ faster than the harness it builds on. On ProgramBench, where agents rebuild programs from scratch, DELM makes faster progress than Claude Code and finishes a 120-minute budget up to 19.9 points higher in test pass rate. The code is available on our project website at https://yuzhenmao.github.io/DeLM/.

passages.summary: 1 Introduction

passages.text: Multi-agent systems (MAS) offer a natural way to scale large language model reasoning at test time: instead of solving a complex task in a single trajectory, they decompose it into subtasks, dispatch agents in parallel, and aggregate their progress (Anthropic, 2026, Feng et al., 2026, Hong et al., 2023, Kimi et al., 2026, OpenAI, 2025, Ruan et al., 2026, Zhang et al., 2025). This paradigm is increasingly important in agentic coding, both in repository-level software engineering (e.g., SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), DeepSWE (Huang and Jiang, 2026)), where agents can investigate different files, root causes, or fixes concurrently, and in interactive terminal tasks (e.g., Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026)), where agents can explore alternative solution paths while sharing what they learn about the environment. In both settings, the value of MAS lies not in issuing more model calls, but in converting additional test-time compute into useful parallel progress, reducing wall-clock time and improving success rates without a proportional increase in cost.

Borrowing a term from pipeline parallelism (Huang et al., 2019), we call agent time that does not advance the solution a _bubble_ : time an agent spends waiting on others, or redoing work a peer has already done. Bubbles waste compute and stretch wall-clock time, and each of the three dominant families of MAS creates them in its own way.

passages.text: **Independent agents** run in parallel and select among their outputs, as in self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022), repeated sampling (Brown et al., 2024), and best-of- _n_ sampling (Cobbe et al., 2021, Lightman et al., 2024). They never wait, but they share nothing while they run, so each agent must rediscover the same faults, fixes, and dead ends on its own. Their bubbles are _redundant work_ : adding agents adds compute, but much of it repeats exploration another agent has already done.

passages.text: **Peer-communicating agents** exchange responses over synchronous rounds, as in multi-agent debate (Chen et al., 2024, Du et al., 2023, Liang et al., 2023). Seeing peers’ answers lets agents correct one another, but each round is a barrier: its duration is set by the slowest agent, so agents that finish early sit idle. These _barrier waits_ are the straggler problem familiar from bulk-synchronous parallel computing (Dean and Ghemawat, 2008, Valiant, 1990). Communication cost also grows with the number of agents: in the fully connected setting (Du et al., 2023), each agent ingests all _n −_ 1 peer responses every round, for _n_ ( _n −_ 1) messages per round, so each agent’s context fills with peer responses it must read and reconcile on its own.

passages.text: **Centralized orchestration** underlies structured reasoning methods (Besta et al., 2024, Ning et al., 2024, Yao et al., 2023), SPRINT (Biju et al., 2026), the native subagents of Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026) and Codex (OpenAI, 2025), AOrchestra (Ruan et al., 2026), and blackboard-style systems with a control agent (Han and Zhang, 2025, Salemi et al., 2025). A main agent decomposes the task, dispatches subtasks, waits for their outputs, and integrates the results (Figure 2, left). This parallelizes sub-agent execution but not the coordination around it, creating _relay bubbles_ : the main agent idles while delegated work runs, and sub-agents, unaware of one another, cannot build on each other’s progress until the main agent relays it. On Terminal-Bench 4.0’s retro-console-soc task (Figure 3), Claude Code’s main agent spends 73% of its time waiting on its subagents. Relaying can also lose information. Because progress lives in the main agent’s context, details can be dropped in summarization, and correcting an error that has already propagated requires another round of delegation.

passages.text: Figure 2 compares centralized and decentralized multi-agent systems. On the left, the centralized model shows a main agent that reads from a global context and writes back to it, while acting as the sole coordinator for sub-agents. The main agent assigns subtasks and subcontexts to the sub-agents and then integrates their returned results, a process described as rigid and bottlenecked. On the right, the decentralized model, called DeLM, replaces the main agent with a shared context and a task queue. Parallel agents asynchronously claim tasks from the queue and publish findings to the shared context, allowing them to build on or correct each other's progress. This approach is described as adaptive and scalable.

passages.text: We propose **Decentralized Language Models (DELM)** , a MAS framework that squeezes out these bubbles by replacing the main agent with a shared problem state (Figure 2, right). DELM consists of parallel agents, a shared context, and a task queue, and each component targets one kind of bubble. Agents claim tasks from the queue asynchronously, so no agent waits at a round barrier or for a main agent to assign work. They publish compact findings to the shared context as soon as results are available, so peers build on intermediate progress instead of waiting for a relay. The queue and shared context also show what each agent is working on and which approaches have failed, so agents avoid redoing a peer’s work. Finally, corrections are appended as new entries rather than relayed through a main agent, so a fix reaches every agent without another round of delegation. Table 1 contrasts these mechanisms with those of the systems we compare against. On Terminal-Bench 4.0’s retro-console-soc task (Figure 3), four DELM agents spend only 2% of their time waiting and finish 5.5 _×_ sooner than Claude Code with native subagents.

In step 2, Parallel Agents claim subtasks, such as T 1, T 2, and T 3, from this queue. These agents read from a Shared Context and implement their assigned subtasks locally. passages.text: The shared context _C_ is an append-only log of reusable findings and contributions from all agents. Agents write to it through compact entries _G<sub>i</sub>_ of a declared type: a FACT records a finding supported by observations, a FAIL records an approach or hypothesis that was contradicted, and a completion summary records the result of a finished subtask. FACT and FAIL entries carry explicit scope and evidence fields; agents are instructed to keep entries brief and to state unfinished parts and known limitations, so that other agents can judge whether an entry applies to their own work. Any entry may attach files, which peers can inspect as diffs or merge into their own workspaces with conflict protection. Agents publish an entry as soon as a result is usable and then continue with their own work.

passages.text: **Summaries with files by reference.** An entry can attach files, which are stored separately from its summary and snapshotted at publication time. Agents inspect these files with expand, which shows them as diffs against the original task files, and copy selected files into their own workspace with apply. apply refuses to overwrite local changes it cannot account for, leaving reconciliation to the receiving agent. A read of _C_ shows only what is new since that agent’s last read, namely new entries and changed work status, while older entries remain retrievable on demand. This design resembles demand paging in an operating system: agents follow progress through compact summaries and fetch detailed content from backing storage only when they need it (Appendix A.1).

A FAIL stays open until it is addressed, and before submitting, each agent reads the shared context and resolves any published failure relevant to its own solution.

passages.summary: 2.2 Task Queue

passages.text: The task queue _T_ divides the work among agents. Each item consists of a subject and a free-text detail, in which agents are instructed to state the intended output, its available inputs, the interface it shares with other work, and the earliest partial result it depends on. Agents are instructed to create items only for required implementation, repair of a demonstrated defect, or a concrete open question the solution depends on. At startup, the first agent reserves its own scope and publishes complementary items for its peers, or states the dependency that prevents a split; if it ends before this handoff, the next running agent takes over. After that, any agent can add items or claim open ones at any time. There is no privileged planner and no plan-closure step.

passages.text: **Claims and status.** The queue enforces exclusive claims: the first claim wins, and each agent holds at most one unfinished claim. Every item is marked open, claimed, or done, together with its owner, so each agent can see who is responsible for what and how much remains. Each read also shows every agent’s session state (starting, running, or ended), tracked by the framework rather than reported by the agents. Agents use this state to choose complementary work and to handle dependencies. If a dependency’s owner is starting or running, an agent continues with independent work and waits only when nothing else remains, using a bounded wait that returns as soon as a peer publishes or ends. If the owner of an item has ended without completing it, this does not block progress: an agent that needs the result builds it in its own workspace, reusing anything the owner already shared, instead of waiting.

Each read also shows every agent’s session state (starting, running, or ended), tracked by the framework rather than reported by the agents. Agents use this state to choose complementary work and to handle dependencies. If a dependency’s owner is starting or running, an agent continues with independent work and waits only when nothing else remains, using a bounded wait that returns as soon as a peer publishes or ends. If the owner of an item has ended without completing it, this does not block progress: an agent that needs the result builds it in its own workspace, reusing anything the owner already shared, instead of waiting.

passages.text: **When agents publish and read.** Apart from session state, which the framework tracks automatically, all content in the shared context and task queue comes from the agents themselves: the framework never publishes on an agent’s behalf. Agents decide when to publish and read under the instructions in Appendix E. An agent publishes when a result can unblock a peer, without needing to run new checks first, and avoids routine status updates and repeated evidence. It reads the shared context at startup, before starting a new subproblem or diagnostic hypothesis, before final integration, and before submitting. How often an agent publishes and reads is therefore driven mainly by its own progress rather than by the number of peers.

passages.text: **Benchmarks.** We evaluate DELM on four agentic coding benchmarks. (1) **Terminal-Bench 4.0** (Merrill et al., 2026). The benchmark consists of tasks that agents solve in live terminal environments, such as configuring systems, installing dependencies, and debugging failures. The tasks require long sequences of shell commands and agents benefit from sharing discovered environment state and failed attempts. (2) **DeepSWE v1.1** (Huang and Jiang, 2026). The benchmark contains long-horizon software-engineering tasks. Agents must localize faults, understand interdependent modules, and debug across large codebases. It tests whether agents can reuse each other’s localization and debugging progress instead of repeating it. (3) **SWE-bench Verified** (Jimenez et al., 2024). The benchmark is built from real-world GitHub issues, with human-verified task specifications and tests. Agents inspect the repository, identify the relevant files, implement a fix, and validate it through tests. (4) ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026a). Each task gives the agent a compiled executable and its documentation, and asks it to re-implement the program from scratch. Submissions are scored by hidden behavioral tests that compare the candidate against the original program. We test ProgramBench on two hard tasks, ctags and pandoc, and track the test pass rate over a fixed 120-minute budget. Because DELM targets long-horizon tasks where coordination matters, we evaluate on a subset of long-running tasks from Terminal-Bench 4.0 and DeepSWE v1.1. We select tasks based on the wall-clock latency of Codex with GPT-6-Astra: for Terminal-Bench 4.0, we select 10 tasks with latency between 15 minutes and 1 hour; for DeepSWE v1.1, we select 10 tasks with latency of at least 10 minutes. The full list of selected tasks is provided in Appendix B.

passages.text: **Baselines.** We compare DELM with production coding agent harnesses, both in their default mode and with their native subagents enabled, as well as with a research centralized multi-agent system. **Codex** (v0.153.4) (OpenAI, 2025) and **Claude Code** (v2.1.280) (Anthropic, 2026) are agentic coding harnesses that enable language models to work on coding tasks using tools for file editing and shell execution. **Codex (subagent)** and **Claude Code (subagent)** use the same harnesses, with one addition: the task prompt ends with the instruction “Use [Codex/Claude Code]’s native subagents to help solve this task.” This lets the main agent spawn and coordinate sub-agents through each harness’s built-in mechanism. **AOrchestra** (Ruan et al., 2026) is a centralized multi-agent system. Its main orchestrator creates specialized sub-agents on demand and instantiates each one as a tuple of instruction, context, tools, and model. On SWE-bench Verified, we also compare with **mini-SWEagent** (Yang et al., 2024), a lightweight software-engineering agent that uses a simple linear loop with Bash as its main interface.

passages.text: **Metrics.** We report task accuracy, wall-clock latency, and cost. Wall-clock latency is the time from the first API call to the last generated token. We use two cost measures: Cost/Task is the total API cost of all agents in a single run, and Cost/Submission divides this total by the number of agents, since each DELM agent produces its own submission that is scored independently. All results are averaged over three runs and reported as mean _±_ standard deviation.

passages.text: We evaluate on the 10 long-horizon Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks described in Appendix B. Table 2 shows that DELM improves both accuracy and latency under both base models. With GPT-6-Astra, DELM ( _n_ = 2) reaches 85.00% accuracy, 13.3 points higher than the strongest baseline (Codex and Codex with subagents, both 71.67%), and runs 1 _._ 54 _×_ faster than Codex, at a higher Cost/Task ($13.65 vs. $9.01) but a lower Cost/Submission ($6.83). With Claude Opus 5.5, DELM ( _n_ = 2) reaches 93.33%, 11.7 points above Claude Code, while cutting latency from 130.75 to 64.77 minutes (2 _._ 02 _×_ ) at a lower Cost/Task ($17.91 vs. $20.31).

passages.text: Increasing to _n_ =4 gives the largest speedups (2 _._ 05 _×_ and 2 _._ 49 _×_ ): more work proceeds in parallel, and findings reach peers earlier. It also gives the lowest Cost/Submission, since each agent does a smaller share of the work and total cost grows more slowly than the number of submissions. Accuracy drops by 3–4 points relative to _n_ =2, because each agent still submits a complete solution while building less of it itself. More of each solution is assembled from peers’ components, which raises the risk of integration errors and lets a defect in one shared result affect several submissions. _n_ =4 nonetheless remains above every baseline.

passages.text: Native subagent baselines give model-dependent trade-offs in accuracy and latency, but they consistently raise cost. Codex (subagent) matches vanilla Codex in accuracy and runs 1.34 _×_ faster, but at 2.9 _×_ the cost ($25.80 vs. $9.01). Claude Code with subagents lowers accuracy from 81.67% to 80.00% while increasing latency and raising cost by 1.5 _×_ ($30.88 vs. $20.31). The trajectories show that delegation adds work rather than dividing it. Subagents unaware of one another repeat parts of the same investigation; and the main agent adds further rounds of testing and review while remaining responsible for integration and final delivery. In contrast, DELM ( _n_ =2) costs less per task than either subagent baseline ($13.65 and $17.91) because it keeps communication cheap and makes knowledge reuse direct.

Table 2 compares performance on Terminal-Bench 4.0 across two base models, GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, measuring average accuracy, average latency, cost per task, and cost per submission. Cost per task sums the costs of all agents in a single run, while cost per submission divides this total by the number of agents.

For GPT-6-Astra, DELM with n equals 2 achieves the highest accuracy at 85.00 percent, compared to 71.67 percent for Codex and Codex with subagents, and 70.00 percent for AOrchestra. passages.text: These results show that multiple agents help even on largely sequential tasks. A single agent rarely completes every step correctly on its first attempt. It often inspects irrelevant files, pursues a wrong root cause, or submits a patch that fails the tests before it recovers. Each such detour costs time, and a single agent can only discover it by paying that cost itself. In DELM, agents explore different paths in parallel and record what they learn in the shared context. Once one agent has hit a dead end, the others can skip it, and once one has localized a fault, the others can build on that finding. This shortens the path to a correct fix, which explains why DELM is both faster and more accurate. A more detailed analysis is provided in Appendix D.

There is no natural stopping point: the pass rate keeps rising for as long as agents keep implementing. We therefore use it to ask a different question from the preceding sections: given a fixed wall-clock budget, how much progress does each system make, and how quickly? We run Claude Code and DELM, built on top of Claude Code, with Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh reasoning effort) on two hard tasks, ctags and pandoc. Each run has a 120-minute budget, and we track the hidden-test pass rate over time (Figure 5).

passages.text: To understand how the coordination mechanisms in Table 1 squeeze out bubbles, we analyze all DELM runs on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and DeepSWE v1.1. Parallel subtask execution lets agents build components concurrently (§4.1). Intermediate-results sharing lets agents start dependent work before a peer finishes, avoiding relay waits (§4.2). Peer-status awareness keeps agents from duplicating a peer’s search, avoiding redundant work (§4.3). Finally, a stateful shared context lets corrections reach every agent without another round of delegation, while staying small enough to read cheaply (§4.4).

passages.text: Parallel agents speed up a task only if the work is divided so that no agent idles or duplicates a peer. DELM agents claim distinct components from the task queue, share their code through the shared context, and each integrates its peers’ components into its own solution. Adding agents makes this division finer and shortens the critical path.

passages.text: Parallel agents that cannot see each other’s work tend to converge on the same promising direction. DELM exposes every agent’s claims, status, and stated scope through the task queue and shared context, so an agent can notice an overlap while its search is still running and redirect.

passages.text: Shared results help only if later improvements reach the agents that already used them. Because updates and corrections are appended as new entries that reference revised files, rather than overwriting old ones (§2.1), an agent can re-import a peer’s updated work at any time. Agents rely on this heavily. Across 720 agent trajectories on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and DeepSWE v1.1, agents imported shared files 5,237 times, and 80.3% of trajectories later imported a revised version of a file they had already imported. Agents thus track their peers’ work as it improves, and fixes reach every agent that depends on them without re-planning. In centralized systems, by contrast, correcting a result that has already been summarized and relayed requires another round of delegation.

passages.summary: 5 Related Work

passages.text: **Multi-agent coordination.** Recent LLM-based multi-agent systems improve performance by decomposing tasks across specialized or interacting agents. CAMEL (Li et al., 2023) instantiates role-playing agents to study autonomous cooperation, while MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023) and ChatDev (Qian et al., 2024) organize collaboration through software-engineering roles and standardized workflows. More recent systems make orchestration adaptive. AOrchestra (Ruan et al., 2026) creates task-specific sub-agents on demand, ToolOrchestra (Su et al., 2025) trains a lightweight orchestrator to coordinate models and tools, Squeeze Evolve (Maheswaran et al., 2026) routes the stages of evolutionary inference to models of different cost and capability, and RecursiveMAS (Yang et al., 2026b) replaces text-level communication with recursive latent-state transfer. These systems coordinate through either a fixed workflow or a central orchestrator that decides what each agent sees and when progress is merged. Combee (Li et al., 2026) likewise identifies centralized aggregation as a bottleneck under high parallelism, but addresses it for parallel prompt learning rather than agent coordination.

passages.text: **Blackboard and shared-memory architectures.** Blackboard architectures coordinate problem solvers through a shared workspace (Erman et al., 1980, Nii, 1986). Recent LLM variants use a blackboard on which agents post messages for general reasoning (Han and Zhang, 2025) or to which agents volunteer information in response to requests for data discovery (Salemi et al., 2025). However, these systems still rely on a control agent to select which agent acts or which request is posted, and they treat the board mainly as a message channel. DELM removes the controller from the loop entirely. Agents claim work asynchronously from a task queue, see what their peers are working on, and build on or correct earlier findings by appending to a stateful shared context (Table 1). We further target long-horizon agentic coding, where shared progress includes repository and environment state rather than only textual messages.

passages.text: **Agentic coding harnesses.** Language models become far more capable when coupled with executable environments that let them inspect state, invoke tools, and act on feedback. SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) and its lightweight variant mini-SWE-agent show that a well-designed agent-computer interface substantially improves software-engineering performance. Production harnesses such as Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026) and Codex (OpenAI, 2025) let models read repositories, edit files, execute commands, and increasingly delegate work to native subagents. Recursive Language Models (Zhang et al., 2025) apply a similar code-mediated loop to long-context reasoning by treating the prompt as an external environment. DELM complements these harnesses: rather than replacing the single-agent loop, it adds a coordination layer on top of it, and we instantiate it on both Codex and Claude Code.

passages.summary: 6 Discussion and Limitations

passages.text: **Conclusion.** We introduced DELM, a decentralized multi-agent framework in which agents coordinate through a shared context and a task queue rather than through a main agent. By letting agents claim work asynchronously, publish findings as soon as they are usable, and see what every peer is doing, DELM squeezes out the bubbles that existing designs create: redundant work among independent agents, barrier waits among peer-communicating agents, and relay waits under centralized orchestration. Across Terminal-Bench 4.0, DeepSWE v1.1, and SWE-bench Verified, DELM is both more accurate and faster than single-agent harnesses, their native subagents, and AOrchestra, and on ProgramBench it makes more progress than Claude Code under the same time budget. Our ablation shows that these gains come from coordination rather than parallelism alone: removing any single mechanism brings two agents back to roughly single-agent speed. These results suggest that scaling multi-agent systems requires not only more agents, but a coordination substrate that keeps every agent productive while keeping the cost of communication among them low.

passages.text: DELM is designed for long-horizon tasks, where multiple agents have enough time to share progress and split up the remaining work. On short tasks, a single agent often finishes before any coordination can pay off. We therefore evaluate on a subset of long-running tasks from Terminal-Bench 4.0 and DeepSWE v1.1. We first ran the Codex baseline with GPT-6-Astra (xhigh reasoning effort) on each benchmark and recorded the wall-clock latency of every task. From Terminal-Bench 4.0, we selected 10 tasks whose latency fell between 15 minutes and 1 hour. The upper bound excludes tasks that run so long that repeated evaluation would be impractical. From DeepSWE v1.1, we selected 10 tasks with latency of at least 10 minutes. The selection criterion is based only on the baseline’s latency. Table 7 lists the selected tasks together with their Codex latencies.

passages.text: LongBench-v2 (Bai et al., 2025) is a long-context benchmark designed to evaluate deep understanding and reasoning over realistic tasks. We focus on its multi-document QA setting, which contains 125 samples across diverse domains: Financial (15 samples), Government (23 samples), Multi-News (23 samples), Legal (14 samples), and Academic (50 samples). This setting is also suitable for our evaluation because its questions require multi-hop reasoning over evidence distributed across long contexts, rather than extracting a single local span.

passages.text: Recursive Language Models (RLMs) (Zhang et al., 2025) process long contexts by recursively selecting context segments, issuing sub-calls, and composing the resulting partial answers. Crucially, RLM performs this process through a code-mediated Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL): the long input is stored as an external variable that the model can inspect, parse, and aggregate programmatically. This makes RLM a natural fit for OOLONG (Bertsch et al., 2025), an aggregation-heavy benchmark where each sample consists of timestamped, user-attributed entries and answering a question often requires classifying many entries before computing a distributional answer.

passages.text: We first evaluate DELM and RLM separately on both LongBench-v2 Multi-Doc QA and OOLONG using GPT-5 with medium reasoning (RLM uses GPT-5-mini for sub-calls and recursion depth=1). As shown in Table 9, the two methods have complementary strengths. On LongBench-v2, DELM achieves higher average accuracy than RLM at roughly the same cost per task. On OOLONG, however, DELM underperforms RLM in both average accuracy and cost. This is because OOLONG is closer to a structured data-processing benchmark than a conversational reasoning benchmark (such as LongBench-v2): many questions require exact counting, filtering, comparison, and tie handling. In this setting, the natural-language shared context used by DELM is not reliable. RLM performs better because its core interface is code-mediated: through a REPL environment, the model can inspect, parse, transform, and aggregate the input using executable programs and programmatic sub-calls. However, RLM still relies on centralized coordination, where recursive calls report back to a root process that must reconcile and aggregate their outputs. This centralized aggregation is less suitable for natural-language multi-document reasoning, helping explain RLM’s weaker LongBench-v2 performance. These results motivate a hybrid design that combines RLM’s precise REPL-based execution with DELM’s decentralized coordination.

passages.text: We therefore combine the two methods by retaining RLM as the underlying reasoner while adding two DELM components: a shared context and a decentralized task queue. In this hybrid setting, there is no main-agent/sub-agent hierarchy; all agents are equally ranked RLM instances that coordinate through shared state. An initial RLM call produces a compact work plan, after which subtasks are placed into the task queue and claimed by parallel RLM workers. Each worker’s output is admitted into the shared context, and the system then generates any additional subtasks from the current problem state, and computes the final answer from the shared context once no further subtasks are needed. This design preserves RLM’s strength in precise code-mediated execution while adding DELM’s decentralized coordination. Name the missing input in status and inspect the returned board view before deciding to wait. Do not batch that response with a blocking wait that hides it. If still needed, use read --wait 25 (--for ID when known) with yield_time_ms: 30000, reassessing each returned view before waiting again. Never use sleep, repeated polling, duplicate probes, redundant checks or paperwork to fill the gap. Never wait for an ended peer or a nonrequired addition.

passages.text: Run necessary long diagnostics asynchronously when useful independent work remains, exposing intermediate results. Preserve their inputs and code; results apply to those versions. Read new output when it can change a decision instead of repeatedly polling. If a peer update could make a tool wait unnecessary, read the board before blocking, not after the wait in the same call. Avoid competing workload during timing measurements. Wait only for evidence still required for completion.

passages.text: - Queue items are for required implementation, repair of a demonstrated defect, or a concrete unanswered question needed to implement the solution. Do not create separate verification, testing, review, reproduction, or solution-checker assignments, including at a peer’s request. This rule applies to queue items created with publish or reserve. Diagnosis and measurements needed to choose or repair an implementation remain allowed. A checker that is itself the requested product is implementation.

passages.text: - After the initial handoff, claim an existing item when it fits; otherwise reserve a distinct required implementation scope. Respect the returned owner. Ownership covers an output, not a fixed algorithm. Publish a needed component when a peer can implement it independently, stating its interface, inputs and nonoverlapping scope while continuing your part. Keep small local adjustments under the current claim. Routine local integration and necessary checking need no separate item or active claim. Respect ownership and interfaces while the owner is running. Report concrete defects through scoped FAIL notes. To hand off incomplete work, close the claim with its remaining scope and reusable files. An ended worker’s claim stays with it, but cannot block you from completing required work. Keep completed items closed. Do not assign verification roles through notes or status. Requests for existing evidence and interface clarification remain useful. Initial planning does not make either worker a permanent coordinator or checker. There is no global plan-closure step.

passages.summary: # **Submission.**

passages.text: Before submitting, read the board and address published corrections relevant to your final local solution. A required repair is a dependency even if an earlier artifact is usable. Do not finish with a known unresolved failure of a required behavior or performance target. Once applicable evidence supports satisfying all requirements and no relevant failure remains, preserve that candidate and submit. An optional stronger result or an already-running search is not a reason to delay. Prevent exploratory work from changing the submitted output. Close any claim you still hold with done. If your item is already done, publish required corrections in a note rather than opening a claim merely to finish it. Submit a concise answer with required explanations and known limitations. A peer still working does not block a complete local submission.
